Two countries on this map declared war on birds.

Both lost. One of them lost so badly it helped deepen a famine.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Australia, 1932. Around 20,000 emus moved into the wheat belt of Western Australia after the breeding season, wrecking crops and fences. Farmers, many of them WWI veterans, asked the Defence Minister for machine guns. He said yes.

2/ A small party under Major G.P.W. Meredith deployed with two Lewis guns and roughly 10,000 rounds. The emus split into small groups at the first burst, ran faster than anyone expected, and turned out to be very hard to kill with automatic fire.

3/ The operation was called off, restarted, and wound up in December. The official tally was about 986 birds, perhaps 2,500 counting those that later died of wounds. Meredith is said to have praised the emus' discipline in the field.

4/ China, 1958. The Four Pests Campaign targeted rats, flies, mosquitoes and sparrows. Villagers banged pots and pans to keep sparrows airborne until they dropped from exhaustion, tore down nests and shot them. Numbers collapsed nationwide.

5/ Sparrows ate grain — but they also ate insects. With the birds gone, locust and pest outbreaks followed. By 1960 Beijing had quietly dropped sparrows from the list, swapped in bed bugs, and imported sparrows from the Soviet Union.

6/ The Great Chinese Famine of 1959–61 killed tens of millions. Its main drivers were collectivisation, punishing grain procurement quotas and Great Leap Forward industrial targets — but the missing sparrows made a catastrophe worse.

7/ Two governments, two continents, the same lesson learned twice: ecosystems are much harder to command than armies.
